extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent applicants/attorneys
extracted.subtask_description: Official USPTO guidance for examiners (and practitioners) on the standards for receiving, entering, and weighing affidavits/declarations and other evidence traversing rejections under 37 CFR 1.132, including objective indicia (secondary considerations) of nonobviousness and procedural timeliness rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affidavit/Declaration required for evidence traversing rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: When any claim is rejected or objected to, any evidence submitted to traverse the rejection or objection on a basis not otherwise provided for must be by way of an oath or declaration under 37 CFR 1.132.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An affidavit is a written statement under oath before an authorized official; 37 CFR 1.68 permits a declaration instead of an affidavit. Declarations must include an acknowledgment referencing 18 U.S.C. 1001 and must state which statements are from the declarant’s own knowledge and which are on information and belief. Publications may be evidence if probative and properly submitted. All affidavits/declarations not falling under other specific rules are treated under this rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary examiner responsibility to review and decide sufficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the responsibility of the primary examiner to personally review and decide whether affidavits or declarations and other evidence submitted for the purpose of traversing grounds of rejection are responsive and present sufficient facts to overcome the rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must consider publications to the extent probative, enter timely evidence, acknowledge and comment on entered affidavits/declarations in the next action, and explain specifically when evidence is insufficient. Examiner commentary should be consistent with guidelines for statements of reasons for allowance when the evidence overcomes the prima facie case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of form paragraphs 7.65 and 7.66 for Office actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Form paragraph 7.65 should be used where an affidavit/declaration is effective to withdraw a rejection; form paragraph 7.66 where it is insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form paragraphs include bracketed fields to be filled (type affidavit/declaration; filing date; affected claims; rejection overcome or not overcome with statutory grounds). When 7.66 is used, examiners must follow with detailed reasons for insufficiency (e.g., untimely; fails to set forth facts; facts not germane; not commensurate in scope with claims) and may append subparagraphs 7.66.01–7.66.05 as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasons for insufficiency — ¶7.66.01: Affiant has never seen invention before
rubrics_metrics.description: Affidavit includes statements amounting to an affirmation that the affiant has never seen the claimed subject matter before.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such statements are irrelevant to nonobviousness and provide no objective evidence. This form paragraph must be preceded by form paragraph 7.66 and a full explanation should be provided if appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasons for insufficiency — ¶7.66.02: Invention works as intended
rubrics_metrics.description: Affidavit includes statements affirming that the claimed subject matter functions as intended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statements that the invention works as intended are not relevant to nonobviousness and provide no objective evidence. Must be preceded by form paragraph 7.66 and include a full explanation when used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasons for insufficiency — ¶7.66.03: Refers only to invention, not to claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Affidavit refers only to the system described in the application and not to the individual claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such declarations fail to show objective evidence commensurate in scope with the claims. Must be preceded by form paragraph 7.66 and a full explanation provided if appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasons for insufficiency — ¶7.66.04: No evidence of long-felt need
rubrics_metrics.description: Affidavit states the claimed subject matter solved a long-standing problem but provides no showing that others were working on the problem or evidence they could not solve it despite knowledge of cited references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Must be preceded by form paragraph 7.66 and accompanied by a full explanation. See MPEP § 716.04 for related guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasons for insufficiency — ¶7.66.05: Conclusion that evidence fails to outweigh obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Conclusion that, when all evidence is considered, the totality of rebuttal evidence fails to outweigh the evidence of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as a conclusion to the explanation of insufficiency and must be preceded by form paragraph 7.66.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness of evidence traversing rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence traversing rejections must be timely or seasonably filed to be entered and entitled to consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affidavits/declarations and other evidence are timely if submitted (1) prior to a final rejection; (2) before appeal in an application not having a final rejection; (3) after final rejection but before or on the same date as filing an appeal upon showing good and sufficient reasons under 37 CFR 1.116(e); or (4) after prosecution is closed if filed with an RCE under 37 CFR 1.114 for utility/plant apps filed on or after June 8, 1995, or a CPA under 37 CFR 1.53(d) in a design application. For affidavits filed after appeal see 37 CFR 41.33(d) and MPEP §§ 1206, 1211.03.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration and entry of timely evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence traversing rejections, when timely presented, must be considered and entered by the examiner; all entered affidavits/declarations must be acknowledged and commented upon in the next action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The extent of commentary depends on the action taken: if evidence overcomes the prima facie case, comments should match guidelines for reasons for allowance; if insufficient, the examiner must specifically explain why. General conclusory statements without support are insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective evidence of nonobviousness (secondary considerations) must be considered
rubrics_metrics.description: Affidavits/declarations containing evidence of criticality or unexpected results, commercial success, long‑felt but unsolved needs, failure of others, skepticism of experts, etc., must be considered in determining obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secondary considerations ‘must always when present be considered en route to a determination of obviousness.’ Such evidence may illuminate circumstances surrounding the invention’s origin and be relevant indicia for (un)obviousness. See related case law cited (e.g., Stratoflex, Graham).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of comparative data in the specification
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners must consider comparative data in the specification intended to illustrate the claimed invention when reaching a conclusion on obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparative data can be probative of unexpected results; lack of such objective data does not, by itself, weigh in favor of obviousness, but failure to rebut a prima facie case is dispositive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to provide rebuttal evidence when prima facie case exists is dispositive
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a prima facie case of obviousness is established, the failure to provide rebuttal evidence is dispositive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if objective evidence is absent, that absence does not itself show obviousness; rather, absence of rebuttal when a prima facie case is made is dispositive against patentability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nexus requirement for secondary considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: To be probative, any secondary evidence must be related to the claimed invention — a factually and legally sufficient connection (nexus) is required between the objective evidence and the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weight given depends on relevance and amount/nature of evidence. The applicant/patent owner bears the burden of establishing nexus. Nexus is presumed when the product tied to the evidence includes the claimed features and is coextensive with them; otherwise the patentee may still prove nexus by showing the evidence is the direct result of the unique characteristics of the claimed invention. Evidence resulting from unclaimed or prior-art features lacks nexus. Examiners should evaluate nexus with attention to coextensiveness and whether the indicia are directed to what was not known in the prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probative value: objective evidence must be supported by proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Objective evidence (unexpected results, commercial success, solution of long‑felt need, inoperability of prior art, invention before date of reference, allegations of derivation) must be factually supported by an appropriate affidavit or declaration to be probative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law requires factual evidence (e.g., experimental data) for claims of unexpected results; conclusory assertions without tests/comparisons are insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arguments cannot substitute for evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments presented by the applicant cannot take the place of evidence in the record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statements about unexpected results, commercial success, long‑felt need, inoperability, or derivation must be supported by affidavits/declarations or other factual evidence; see MPEP § 2145 for related case law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opinion evidence: weight and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Factual expert testimony may be considered and given some weight so long as the opinion is not on the ultimate legal conclusion; opinions lacking factual support or on the ultimate legal issue are not entitled to weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must consider (a) the nature of the matter sought to be established, (b) strength of opposing evidence, (c) the expert’s interest in the outcome, and (d) presence/absence of factual support. Expert opinions formulated before the invention and supported by documentary evidence receive greater deference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probative value of commercial success and long‑felt need — potential discounting
rubrics_metrics.description: Objective evidence of commercial success or long‑felt need may be given less weight if the record shows the applicant or patent owner has strong market power or a blocking patent that could deter others from commercializing the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blocking patents may explain lack of others’ development and thus reduce weight of commercial-success evidence. Examiners should articulate reasons for any discounting in Office actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weighing objective evidence against the prima facie case
rubrics_metrics.description: When applicant timely submits rebuttal evidence, the examiner must reconsider patentability and weigh the entire record; evidence supporting patentability must be weighed against evidence supporting the prima facie case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Final determination of patentability is by preponderance of the evidence. Each piece of rebuttal evidence should be evaluated in the context of facts underlying the prima facie case, not merely against the conclusion. If examiner remains unconvinced, the next Office action should state this and identify reasons. Any conclusion about whether objective evidence outweighs obviousness and the weights assigned to different indicia should be explained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allegations of unexpected results (716.02)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any differences between the claimed invention and the prior art may yield some differences in properties; the issue is whether the properties differ to such an extent that the difference is truly unexpected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance includes that unexpectedness must be shown (In re Merck & Co. example), the burden is on applicant to prove unexpected results, evidence must be commensurate in scope with the claimed invention, comparison should be with the closest prior art, and claimed advantages may be disclosed or inherent. See MPEP § 716.02(a)–(f) for detailed subpoints on burden, commensurateness, comparison, and weighing expected vs unexpected results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial success (716.03) — commensurateness and derivation
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial success must be commensurate in scope with the claimed invention and must be shown to be derived from the claimed invention to be probative of nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should look for evidence that sales/success are attributable to claimed features rather than other factors. If commercial success is due to an element known in the prior art, no nexus exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Long‑felt need and failure of others (716.04)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence that the claimed invention satisfied a long‑felt need or that others failed to solve the problem may be probative of nonobviousness when properly supported and shown to relate to the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant must show others were working on problem and could not solve it despite knowledge of prior art; mere assertion is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism of experts (716.05)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence showing skepticism of experts regarding the claimed invention can be an objective indicium of nonobviousness when tied to the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Must be supported by factual evidence and show nexus to claimed features; weight depends on factual support and context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copying (716.06)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence that others copied the invention can be objective evidence of nonobviousness if it is shown that copying was of the claimed invention and not of prior‑art features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate that the copying was motivated by the novel aspects of the claimed invention and include evidence linking the copied features to the claim scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inoperability of references (716.07)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence showing inoperability of prior art references may rebut a rejection if supported by factual proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Must include factual tests or data demonstrating that the prior art would not operate as claimed; conclusory assertions insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility and operability of applicant’s disclosure (716.08)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence that the applicant’s disclosure is useful and operable may support patentability where properly supported.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Must be supported by factual evidence; demonstrate that the claimed invention achieves the asserted utility and is operable across the claimed scope as required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of disclosure (716.09)
rubrics_metrics.description: Affidavits/declarations may be evaluated for whether they disclose sufficient facts and documentary evidence to support their assertions relative to the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should assess whether the showing is commensurate in scope with the claims and whether documentary evidence corroborates assertions (including inventorship/derivation issues).

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribution affidavits/declarations to overcome pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 rejections (716.10 / 717 series)
rubrics_metrics.description: Affidavits or declarations may be used to show that material in a reference originated with or was obtained from the inventor (or joint inventor), which can change the prior‑art status of a reference under pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such affidavits are treated under 37 CFR 1.132 for pre‑AIA cases (or 1.130 for current‑AIA exceptions). Examiner examples: if reference authorship matches inventive entity and was published <1 year prior, it may not be prior art; attribution affidavits attempt to convert a differing‑inventive‑entity situation to one where the reference is not prior art. Examiners should follow MPEP examples and procedures when evaluating attribution affidavits.
